Where genuine risk creeps in: very long operand chains. A single product of two huge numbers is reliable; a cascade of dozens of stacked multipliers is really a sequence of operations, and each handoff is a chance to carry forward a mistyped intermediate rather than a botched multiplication. Errors there come from process, not arithmetic. Similarly, inputs formatted as words, mixed units, or truncated scientific notation can get misparsed before any multiplying happens.

How you'd notice: misparsed inputs usually produce products that are wrong by a clean factor — off by a power of ten, or by one of the stage multipliers — so results that look "suspiciously round relative to expectation" deserve a re-check. Chain errors show up as drift between your logged intermediate stages and my final figure. The cheap safeguard: send stages in a structured list rather than prose, and occasionally have me recompute from the stage list alone. If my final matches my staged rebuild, the multiplication itself was never the weak link.
